rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Moved by the warning that the recipient stands between two outcomes, Umar wept and gave his shirt for the Day of Judgment, not because of the poem.
rows.anchor: فبكى عمر حتى اخضلت لحيته

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Giving without seeking repayment or thanks, and without reminding or publicizing the gift, is nobler for the giver and more comfortable for the recipient; seeking repayment makes the giver a trader unworthy of praise.
rows.anchor: قال الماوردي: وإذا كان العطاء على هذا الوجه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads 74:6 as forbidding a gift given in expectation of a larger return.
rows.anchor: وقد قال ابن عباس في قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says this verse concerns those who remain behind from jihad yet spend, while the preceding verse concerns those who go out themselves; Ibn Atiyya rejects this as unsupported conjecture.
rows.anchor: وذهب ابن زيد إلى أن هذه الآية إنما هي في الذين لا يخرجون في الجهاد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya finds Ibn Zayd's allocation of this and the preceding verse to different groups manifestly speculative.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وفي هذا القول نظر لأن التحكم فيه باد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mann is recounting a favor in order to enumerate it and reproach the recipient; another definition is talking about a gift until the recipient hears and is hurt.
rows.anchor: ذكر النعمة على معنى التعديد لها والتقريع بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mann is a major sin; Muslim reports that it is among three whom God will neither regard nor purify and who face painful punishment.
rows.anchor: والمن من الكبائر، ثبت ذلك في صحيح مسلم وغيره

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Ibn Umar transmits a Prophetic warning listing people barred from God's regard and from Paradise, including one who reminds others of what he gave.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One Muslim wording defines the mannan as someone who gives nothing except to hold it over the recipient.
rows.anchor: المنان هو الذي لا يعطي شيئا إلا منة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Harm includes insults and complaints; it is broader than mann, which is singled out because it commonly occurs and is one form of harm.
rows.anchor: السب والتشكي، وهو أعم من المن لأن المن جزء من الأذى

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd advises a donor who thinks even greeting the recipient burdens him to refrain from greeting him.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: لئن ظننت أن سلامك يثقل على من أنفقت عليه

rows.speaker: أبو أسامة
rows.claim: When a woman disparaged fighters as going out to eat fruit and offered arrows and a quiver, Abu Usama said she had harmed them before giving.
rows.anchor: فقال: لا بارك الله في أسهمك وجعبتك فقد آذيتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A donor who avoids reminders and harm, even remarks such as complaining of the recipient's persistence, is guaranteed reward, identified here as Paradise.
rows.anchor: فمن أنفق في سبيل الله ولم يتبعه منا ولا أذى كقوله: ما أشد إلحاحك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The donor is promised security from future fear after death and from grief over worldly losses, since he rejoices in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ونفى عنه الخوف بعد موته لما يستقبل، والحزن على ما سلف من دنياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also supports preferring wealth to poverty, a question the commentary says it will explain later.
rows.anchor: وفيها دلالة لمن فضل الغني على الفقر

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas parses 'kind speech' as an independent phrase with an omitted predicate; alternatively, an omitted subject makes it the commanded response.
rows.anchor: أي قول معروف أولى وأمثل ذكره النحاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kind speech means prayer, reassurance, and encouragement about God's reward; it is better than charity that looks charitable but earns nothing because it is followed by harm.
rows.anchor: الدعاء والتأنيس والترجية بما عند الله

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet calls a good word charity and says meeting one's brother with a cheerful face is an act of kindness; Muslim transmits the report.
rows.anchor: الكلمة الطيبة صدقة وإن من المعروف أن تلقى أخاك بوجه طلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Receive a petitioner warmly and speak gently, so that a gift earns thanks and a refusal is excused.
rows.anchor: ويقابله بالطلاقة والتقريب ليكون مشكورا إن أعطى ومعذورا إن منع

rows.speaker: بعض الحكماء
rows.claim: A sage advises greeting someone in need cheerfully: if he does not thank you, at least he has an excuse for not receiving help.
rows.anchor: بعض الحكماء: الق صاحب الحاجة بالبشر فإن عدمت شكره لم تعدم عذره

rows.speaker: ابن لنكك
rows.claim: Ibn Lankak recounts Ibn Duraid's unsuccessful appeal to a minister and quotes verses urging a patron not to resent petitioners or repel hopeful faces.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن لنكك أن أبا بكر بن دريد قصد بعض الوزراء في حاجة لم يقضها

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report from Umar attributes to the Prophet an instruction to let a petitioner finish, then answer with dignity and gentleness, a small gift, or a gracious refusal; unseen beings observe how God's gifts are used.
rows.anchor: من حديث عمر رضي الله عنه قال قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author links that report to the Muslim narration of an angel testing a leper, a bald man, and a blind man by appearing in their forms.
rows.anchor: حديث أبرص وأقرع وأعمى، خرجه مسلم وغيره

rows.speaker: بشر بن الحارث
rows.claim: In a dream, Bishr asks Ali for useful advice; Ali says wealthy compassion toward the poor seeks God's reward, while poor people's dignity toward the rich rests on trust in God's promise.
rows.anchor: وقال بشر بن الحارث: رأيت عليا في المنام

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In the dream, Ali closes his advice with a poem about inevitable death and building for the lasting afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال بشر بن الحارث: رأيت عليا في المنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here 'forgiveness' means concealing a needy person's deficiency and poor condition; an Arab used the phrase 'God forgive' when shame about his livelihood prevented him from giving his lineage.
rows.anchor: الستر للخلة وسوء حالة المحتاج ومن هذا قول الأعرابي

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash interprets the phrase as forgiving a persistent, rude petitioner, which is better than giving with reproach and injury.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى تجاوز عن السائل إذا ألح وأغلظ وجفى

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says this interpretation is syntactically difficult: 'forgiveness' is the subject and 'better than charity' its predicate, with an implied act leading to forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وقال النحاس: هذا مشكل يبينه الإعراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative parsing makes God's forgiveness better than the particular charity donors spoil with reminders.
rows.anchor: تفضل الله عليك أكبر من الصدقة التي تمن بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is absolutely independent of human charity and commanded it to reward people; His forbearance means He does not punish the donor immediately for reminders and harm.
rows.anchor: أخبر تعالى عن غناه المطلق أنه غني عن صدقة العباد وإنما أمر بها ليثيبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Invalidating' means that the particular charity followed by reminders or harm is not accepted and loses reward; it does not invalidate unrelated good deeds, since sins do not annul good deeds as a general rule.
rows.anchor: الصدقة التي يمن بها ويؤذي، لا غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars say God does not accept a donation when He knows its donor will later reproach or harm the recipient; another view says God gives the recording angel a sign not to record it.
rows.anchor: قال جمهور العلماء في هذه الآية: إن الصدقة التي يعلم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic idiom calls a gift used for reproach a 'black hand,' an unasked gift a 'white hand,' and a gift prompted by a request a 'green hand.'
rows.anchor: ولما يعطي عن غير مسألة: يد بيضاء

rows.speaker: بعض البلغاء
rows.claim: A rhetorician says that reminding someone of a favor forfeits gratitude, while admiring one's own deed destroys its reward.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض البلغاء: من من بمعروفه

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: When Ibn Sirin heard a man enumerate favors to another, he told him to stop: beneficence has no good in it once it is counted aloud.
rows.anchor: وسمع ابن سيرين رجلا يقول لرجل:

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A Prophetic report warns that reminding others of a favor erases gratitude and reward, then recites this verse; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال:

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik disliked paying obligatory alms to relatives for fear of seeking their praise, reminding them, or receiving repayment that compromises sincerity; he preferred strangers and having another distribute it when the ruler is unjust.
rows.anchor: كره مالك لهذه الآية أن يعطي الرجل صدقته الواجبة أقاربه لئلا يعتاض منهم الحمد والثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If voluntary secret charity loses its reward, it simply becomes as though never done; if obligatory alms loses reward, the giver faces a threat as though he failed to perform it.
rows.anchor: وهذا بخلاف صدقة التطوع السر لأن ثوابها إذا حبط سلم من الوعيد وصار في حكم من لم يفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, the comparison's kāf can be accusative as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun or can function circumstantially.
rows.anchor: الكاف في موضع نصب، أي إبطال «كالذي»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harmful donor is compared to a show-off who gives for reputation, like a disbeliever seeking praise; rain strips dust from a smooth rock and exposes its barren surface, just as these motives expose the intention and erase the gift.
rows.anchor: مثل الله تعالى الذي يمن ويؤذي بصدقته بالذي ينفق ماله رئاء الناس لا لوجه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that reminder and harm erase the gift's excellence, not its reward: a show-off earns nothing like a disbeliever, while a sincere donor originally merits reward but loses the gift's excellence.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالآية إبطال الفضل دون الثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says only the reward after the donor begins reminding and harming is lost; earlier reward remains, but further multiplication stops, as charity otherwise grows like a mountain.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إنما يبطل من ثواب صدقته من وقت منه وإيذائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the first interpretation of the preceding disagreement as the more apparent one.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أظهر والله أعلم

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says ṣafwān is a collective with singular ṣafwāna; another reported view treats ṣafwān as singular, like 'stone.'
rows.anchor: جمع واحده صفوانة قاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i calls ṣafwān singular and gives ṣafwān, ṣafī, and ṣafiyy as plurals; al-Mubarrad rejects ṣafī as the plural of ṣafā, like qafā/qafī.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: صفوان واحد وجمعه صفوان وصفي وصفي، وأنكره المبرد

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhri read ṣafwān with a fatḥa on the fāʾ, a dialectal form; Qutrub also records the form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ سعيد بن المسيب والزهري «صفوان» بتحريك الفاء، وهي لغة

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas allows ṣafwān to be singular or plural but judges singular more likely because the verse says dust was on it; he rejects al-Kisa'i's plural analysis as linguistically unsound.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: صفوان وصفوان يجوز أن يكون جمعا ويجوز أن يكون واحدا، إلا أن الأولى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem mentioning the crow's day supports the weak analysis of krawān as a plural of karwān; ṣafī is likewise a plural of ṣafā, like ʿaṣā.
rows.anchor: والضعيف في العربية كروان جمع كروان وصفي وصفي جمع صفا مثل عصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wābil means heavy rain; the same root describes a severe taking in 73:16 and severe blows or punishment.
rows.anchor: والوابل: المطر الشديد. وقد وبلت السماء تبل، والأرض موبولة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Ṣald describes smooth stone that grows nothing; al-Kisa'i gives the verb and adjective forms, including a smooth bald forehead.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: صلد يصلد صلدا بتحريك اللام فهو صلد بالإسكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author describes ṣald as smooth, non-growing stone and gives a smooth bald forehead as an example before citing al-Asmaʿi’s verse.
rows.anchor: هو كل ما لا ينبت شيئا ومنه جبين أصلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'They cannot do anything' refers to the show-off, disbeliever, and donor who reminds recipients: they cannot benefit from the reward of their spending when they need it, because it was for other than God.
rows.anchor: أي على الانتفاع بثواب شيء من إنفاقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending is called their 'earnings' because they intended to acquire a return through it.
rows.anchor: فعبر عن النفقة بالكسب لأنهم قصدوا بها الكسب

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi says the example concerns the show-off losing reward and the donor who reminds losing the excellence of the gift.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ضرب هذا مثلا للمرائي في إبطال ثوابه، ولصاحب المن والأذى في إبطال فضله ذكره الماوردي

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says aṣlad means hairless in the Hudhayl dialect.
rows.anchor: قال النقاش: الأصلد الأجرد بلغة هذيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibtighāʾ is parsed as a purpose complement and tathbītan coordinated with it; Makki treats both as purpose complements, but Ibn Atiyya rejects that analysis for tathbītan because spending is not done for the sake of stabilization.
rows.anchor: قال مكي في المشكل: كلاهما مفعول من أجله. قال ابن عطية: وهو مردود

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says ibtighāʾ is best read as a verbal noun functioning circumstantially, coordinated with the verbal noun tathbītan; purpose accusative remains possible for ibtighāʾ alone.
rows.anchor: «ابتغاء» نصب على المصدر في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning against corrupt charity, the passage now describes spending that flourishes because it follows the law and its proper intent.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر الله تعالى صفة صدقات القوم الذين لا خلاق لصدقاتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibtighāʾ means seeking, and marḍāt is the verbal noun of raḍiya.
rows.anchor: «ابتغاء» معناه طلب. و «مرضات» مصدر من رضي يرضى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Hasan interpret tathbītan as carefully considering where to place charity; al-Hasan describes giving only after confirming the motive is God's.
rows.anchor: «وتثبيتا» معناه أنهم يتثبتون أين يضعون صدقاتهم قاله مجاهد والحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains tathbītan as belief and certainty; he and Qatada also explain it as seeking God's reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه تصديقا ويقينا قاله ابن عباس. وقال ابن عباس أيضا وقتادة: معناه واحتسابا

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Abu Salih, and others understand tathbītan as certainty: insightful souls strengthen a person to spend in obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي والسدي وقتادة أيضا وابن زيد وأبو صالح وغيرهم: «وتثبيتا» معناه وتيقنا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya prefers the certainty, reward-seeking, and confirmation readings over al-Hasan and Mujahid because the latter give the verbal noun a nonliteral sense without an explicit preceding verb.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأقوال الثلاث أصوب من قول الحسن ومجاهد لأن المعنى الذي ذهبا إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says a verbal noun used in a different sense requires an explicit antecedent verb, as in 71:17 and 73:8.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا لا يسوغ إلا مع ذكر المصدر والإفصاح بالفعل المتقدم

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says Mujahid's interpretation would require tathabbatan; Qatada's 'expecting reward' is unfamiliar unless it means that their souls, expecting reward, strengthen them, which he finds far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وقال النحاس: لو كان كما قال مجاهد لكان وتثبتا من تثبت

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas approves al-Sha'bi's sense: one's own certainty strengthens resolve and judgment to spend in obedience to God.
rows.anchor: وقول الشعبي حسن، أي تثبيتا من أنفسهم لهم على إنفاق ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that donors acknowledge God will confirm the reward, unlike a hypocrite who does not expect recompense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «وتثبيتا من أنفسهم» أي يقرون بأن الله تعالى يثبت عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A janna is an orchard, a plot whose trees cover it; the word shares the root of jinn and embryo because they are hidden.
rows.anchor: الجنة: البستان، وهي قطعة أرض تنبت فيها الأشجار حتى تغطيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rabwa is a slightly elevated place, usually with deep soil and better growth, which explains why it is chosen for the parable.
rows.anchor: والربوة: المكان المرتفع ارتفاعا يسيرا، معه في الأغلب كثافة تراب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects al-Tabari's identification with the 'gardens of al-Ḥazn': those are the gardens of Najd, whose growth and air he says are superior to Tihama's.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ورياض الحزن ليست من هذا كما زعم الطبري، بل تلك هي الرياض المنسوبة إلى نجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Arab woman compared her husband to a Tihama night, invoked as evidence that Tihama's air is unpleasant except at night.
rows.anchor: وقلما يصلح هواء تهامة إلا بالليل ولذلك قالت الأعرابية:

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi reads rabwa as rabāwa, a low-lying place; Ibn Atiyya calls the wording awkward, and the author says it is untenable because the root means increase and elevation.
rows.anchor: وقال السدى: «بربوة» أي برباوة، وهو ما انخفض من الأرض

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains 'a severe seizure' in 69:10 as increased and compares it with taking more than one gave, as evidence for the root's sense of increase.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء في قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil defines rabwa as elevated, good land; the author says the verse pictures a raised place without running water, familiar from Arab experience.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: الربوة أرض مرتفعة طيبة وخص الله تعالى بالذكر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas defines rabwa as elevated land without rivers, inferred from the verse's rainfall; it cannot mean only river-fed land because 11:98 mentions a rabwa with stable water and a spring.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الربوة المكان المرتفع الذي لا تجري فيه الأنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In common Arabic, rabwa means any land raised above its surroundings, whether or not water flows there.
rows.anchor: والمعروف من كلام العرب أن الربوة ما ارتفع عما جاوره سواء جرى فيها ماء أو لم يجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first four readings are ḍamma for Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Nafi, and Abu Amr; fatḥa for Asim, Ibn Amir, and al-Hasan; kasra for Ibn Abbas and Abu Ishaq; and rabāwa with fatḥa for Abu Jaʿfar and Abu Abd al-Rahman.
rows.anchor: وفيها خمس لغات «ربوة» بضم الراء، وبها قرأ ابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي ونافع وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣābah refers to the elevated ground; wābil is heavy rain, and the cited poem describes a luxuriant garden watered by a downpour.
rows.anchor: يعني الربوة. { وابل } أي مطر شديد قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ātāt means 'yielded'; ukul is edible fruit, with 14:25 as a parallel; ukla can also mean a bite or two, as in a Muslim report.
rows.anchor: أي أعطت. { أكلها } بضم الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive link to the garden is one of association, like a horse's saddle or a house's door, since the garden itself does not eat fruit.
rows.anchor: وإضافته إلى الجنة إضافة اختاص، كسرج الفرس وباب الدار

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafi, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read ukul with a ḍamma on hamza and a still kāf in feminine possessives; Abu Amr lengthens other contexts where the others lighten, while Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i lengthen all listed forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو «أكلها» بضم الهمزة وسكون الكاف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akl and ukl mean the same thing.
rows.anchor: ويقال: أكل وأكل بمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden yields twice the fruit of other land; the author prefers this over the report that it bears twice yearly, meaning one year's yield equals two years elsewhere.
rows.anchor: أي أعطت ضعفي ثمر غيرها من الأرضين

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad supplies an omitted phrase: if no downpour reaches it, a light rain is enough; al-Zajjaj instead glosses the phrase as the light rain that reaches it.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد وغيره: تقديره فطل يكفيها. وقال الزجاج: فالذي يصيبها طل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tall is light, fine rain according to Ibn Abbas and others; Mujahid and some others identify it with dew, which Ibn Atiyya calls figurative comparison.
rows.anchor: والطل: المطر الضعيف المستدق من القطر الخفيف قاله ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi notes that dew-fed crops yield less than rain-fed crops but retain some growth and benefit.
rows.anchor: قال الماوردي: وزرع الطل أضعف من زرع المطر وأقل ريعا، وفيه وإن قل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some propose inverted word order, making the garden yield after either heavy rain or drizzle; the author prefers the ordinary order and sees no need for inversion.
rows.anchor: قلت: التأويل الأول أصوب ولا حاجة إلى التقديم والتأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable depicts sincere spending growing as God nurtures charity, like a foal or young camel, unlike dust washed off a bare rock.
rows.anchor: فشبه تعالى نمو نفقات هؤلاء المخلصين الذين يربي الله صدقاتهم كتربية الفلو والفصيل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli reads rabāwa with kasra; al-Farra records rabāwa variants and derives them from rising, from rabā yarbū.
rows.anchor: «رباوة» بالكسر، وبها قرأ الأشهب العقيلي. قال الفراء: ويقال برباوة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that God takes a single date from lawful earnings and nurtures it like a colt or young camel until it becomes mountain-sized or greater; Muslim and the Muwatta transmit it.
rows.anchor: لا يتصدق أحد بتمرة من كسب طيب إلا أخذها الله بيمينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's seeing what people do conveys both promise and warning.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { والله بما تعملون بصير } وعد ووعيد

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri reads 'they do' in the third person; the pronoun may refer to people generally or just donors, in which case the statement is pure promise.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري «يعملون» بالياء كأنه يريد به الناس أجمع،

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi, preferred by al-Tabari, takes the garden as a second parable for ostentatious spending; Ibn Abbas also reports a likeness to deeds of show-offs that are void when most needed.
rows.anchor: حكى الطبري عن السدي أن هذه الآية مثل آخر لنفقة الرياء،

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd connects the garden directly to the prohibition against nullifying charity with reminders and harm in 2:264.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن ابن زيد أنه قرأ قول الله تعالى:

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the connection to the preceding context is clearer than treating this as a separate parable for ostentatious spending; more broadly it covers any hypocrite or disbeliever whose apparent good deed vanishes when needed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا أبين من الذي رجح الطبري، وليست هذه الآية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the established Bukhari report, Ibn Abbas says the garden represents a wealthy person who obeys God, then follows Satan into sins until his life's work is burned away; Umar approves the explanation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ضربت مثلا لعمل

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar asks the Companions what the garden verse means, urges them to answer rather than defer, and accepts Ibn Abbas's interpretation; another report says a person may end a righteous life with evil deeds when he most needs his work.
rows.anchor: خرج البخاري عن عبيد بن عمير قال: قال عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن أبي مليكة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Mulayka reports Umar explaining that someone may do good until old age but commit evil at the end of life, when he most needs his good deeds.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن أبي مليكة أن عمر تلا هذه الآية. وقال: هذا مثل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, al-Rabi, and others support a broad reading that applies to every case covered by the wording.
rows.anchor: وبنحو ذلك قال مجاهد وقتادة والربيع وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Palms and grapes are singled out because they are superior and especially prized among trees; 'all fruits' means every kind grows there.
rows.anchor: وخص النخيل والأعناب بالذكر لشرفهما وفضلهما على سائر الشجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past-tense 'old age struck him' is coordinated with the future 'that he should have'; alternative analyses link it to 'would wish,' treat it as circumstantial, or understand an implicit 'if he had a garden.'
rows.anchor: عطف ماضيا على مستقبل وهو «تكون»

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says an iʿṣār with fire is a wind containing intense cold.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: «إعصار فيه نار» ريح فيها برد شديد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines iʿṣār as a powerful whirlwind rising from the ground like a column, called a zawbaʿa.
rows.anchor: الزجاج: الإعصار في اللغة الريح الشديدة التي تهب من الأرض

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari says a whirlwind is also called zawbaʿa or umm zawbaʿa; the term also names a chief of the jinn.
rows.anchor: قال الجوهري: الزوبعة رئيس من رؤساء الجن

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi says the wind is called iʿṣār because it twists like cloth when wrung; Ibn Atiyya calls this weak, but the author endorses it as the observable coiling column.
rows.anchor: المهدوي: قيل لها إعصار لأنها تلتف كالثوب إذا عصر. ابن عطية: وهذا ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author regards the twisting-column explanation as sound because it matches what can be seen.
rows.anchor: المحسوس، فإنه يصعد عمودا ملتفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other derivations say the wind squeezes clouds, or that muʿṣirāt are pregnant clouds or clouds compressed by winds; Ibn Sidah says some took muʿṣirāt to mean winds.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنما قيل للريح إعصار لأنه يعصر السحاب

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi describe the iʿṣār as a violent, scorching wind; Ibn Abbas calls it a wind with intense samūm heat.
rows.anchor: ابن زيد: الإعصار ريح عاصف وسموم شديدة وكذلك قال السدي

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the whirlwind's intense heat or cold is a breath of Hell, citing Prophetic reports about delaying prayer in severe heat and the Fire's complaint.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويكون ذلك في شدة الحر ويكون في شدة البرد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others explain the parable as a disbeliever's or hypocrite's livelihood orchard burning when its elderly owner and weak children can neither replace nor sustain it; the afterlife offers no second chance to restore deeds.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس وغيره: أن هذا مثل ضربه الله تعالى للكافرين والمنافقين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also says the closing appeal is to reflect on the world's passing and the afterlife's arrival and permanence.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: تتفكرون في زوال الدنيا وفنائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appeal to reflect also means returning to God's majesty and lordship rather than taking protectors besides Him.
rows.anchor: يريد كي ترجعوا إلى عظمتي وربوبيتي ولا تتخذوا من دوني أولياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to believers includes the entire community of Muhammad.
rows.anchor: هذا خطاب لجميع أمة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali, Ubayda al-Salmani, and Ibn Sirin say the command concerns obligatory zakat and forbids substituting inferior goods for good ones.
rows.anchor: فقال علي بن أبي طالب وعبيدة السلماني وابن سيرين: هي الزكاة المفروضة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says al-Bara, al-Hasan, and Qatada appear to understand voluntary charity, urging donors to choose good quality; the verse covers both obligatory and voluntary giving.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والظاهر من قول البراء بن عازب والحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The obligatory view relies on the command's force and the specific ban on inferior goods, while the voluntary view says an imperative can recommend and inferior donations are also disfavored because God deserves the best.
rows.anchor: لكن صاحب الزكاة تعلق بأنها مأمور بها والأمر على الوجوب

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Al-Bara reports that the Prophet saw someone hang a bunch of inferior dates and said, 'What a bad thing to hang'; the verse was then revealed. Al-Tirmidhi transmits it, with fuller wording deferred.
rows.anchor: وروى البراء: أن رجلا علق قنو حشف، فرآه رسول الله

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explains 'good things' as lawful earnings; most interpreters instead mean good and selected-quality property.
rows.anchor: وجمهور المتأولين قالوا: معنى «من طيبات» من جيد ومختار «ما كسبتم». وقال ابن زيد:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earnings include wages from bodily labor and proceeds from trade; inheritance also counts as acquisition for the heir.
rows.anchor: الكسب يكون بتعب بدن وهي الإجارة

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn Mubarak advises a person with sufficient subsistence to leave earning even for charitable ends, since earning and spending lawfully will both be questioned; abstaining from lawful gain is zuhd.
rows.anchor: قال سهل بن عبد الله: وسئل ابن المبارك عن الرجل يريد أن يكتسب

rows.speaker: ابن خويزمنداد
rows.claim: Ibn Khuwiz Mindad says the verse permits a father to eat from his child's earnings, citing a Prophetic report continued in the next segment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن خويزمنداد: ولهذه الآية جاز للوالد أن يأكل من كسب ولده

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The cited Prophetic report says children are among one's good earnings and permits eating from their property; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: أولادكم من طيب أكسابكم فكلوا من أموال أولادكم هنيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What God brings from the earth includes three categories: plants, minerals, and buried treasure.
rows.anchor: يعني النبات والمعادن والركاز، وهذه أبواب ثلاثة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports the Prophetic rule that crops below five wasqs owe no zakat; a wasq is sixty sāʿs, so the threshold is 300 sāʿs of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins; vegetables owe none.
rows.anchor: فروى الدارقطني عن عائشة رضي الله عنها قالت: جرت السنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some invoke the verse's general wording to support Abu Hanifa's view that zakat applies to everything the earth produces, in any quantity and category; details are deferred to al-An'am.
rows.anchor: وقد احتج قوم لأبي حنيفة بقول الله تعالى:

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that injury caused by an animal, a well, or a mine is uncompensated, while buried treasure owes one fifth.
rows.anchor: وأما المعدن فروى الأئمة عن أبي هريرة عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars infer that mines and buried treasure have different rules because the hadith separates them with a conjunction; otherwise it would have stated that the mine owes one fifth.
rows.anchor: لما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rikaz linguistically and in the majority's legal usage is gold, silver, or gems embedded in the ground; an unworked nugget found inside a mine owes one fifth, while Malik's first and relied-upon view treats it like mined material requiring labor.
rows.anchor: والركاز أصله في اللغة ما ارتكز بالأرض من الذهب والفضة والجواهر

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report asks the Prophet to define rikaz, and he calls it gold God placed in the earth when He created the heavens and earth; its transmitter Abdullah ibn Said is abandoned, and another route is unsound.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: سئل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الركاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transmitter Abdullah ibn Said is abandoned, and another route for the Abu Hurayra report is unsound, as al-Daraqutni notes.
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن سعيد هذا متروك الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars agree that pre-Islamic buried wealth is rikaz; money buried after Islam is treated as lost property.
rows.anchor: لا يختلفون فيه إذا كان دفنه قبل الإسلام

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik assigns pre-Islamic treasure in certain Arab or peaceful Muslim lands to its finder with a fifth due; treasure in Islamic territory is lost property, conquest land belongs to its conquerors, and treaty land belongs to its residents, with another view giving it to all treaty residents.
rows.anchor: فقال مالك: ما وجد من دفن الجاهلية في أرض العرب أو في فيافي الأرض

rows.speaker: إسماعيل
rows.claim: Ismail says treasure follows the spoils rule because a Muslim finds pagan property as if he had fought and seized it, receiving four fifths.
rows.anchor: قال إسماعيل: وإنما حكم للركاز بحكم الغنيمة لأنه مال كافر وجده مسلم

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qasim recounts Malik changing his position on found objects such as jewelry, iron, and lead: one fifth, then none, and finally one fifth again.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن القاسم: كان مالك يقول في العروض والجواهر والحديد والرصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Malik’s final view that one fifth is due on found valuables is correct, supported by the general hadith and followed by most jurists.
rows.anchor: وهو الصحيح لعموم الحديث وعليه جمهور الفقهاء

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and Muhammad assign treasure found in a house to its owner, with a fifth due; Abu Yusuf and al-Thawri assign it to the finder. In open land all give it to the finder with a fifth, without distinguishing lands.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة ومحمد في الركاز يوجد في الدار: إنه لصاحب الدار دون الواجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Medinese Malikites, al-Layth, Ibn Nafi, al-Shafi'i, and most scholars make no land-based distinction; the finder may keep the fifth if needy or give it to the poor.
rows.anchor: ومن أهل المدينة وأصحاب مالك من لا يفرق بين شيء من ذلك وقالوا: سواء وجد الركاز

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik and his followers impose zakat on mined gold or silver once it reaches twenty mithqals or five awāq; additional extraction is counted while the vein continues, but a new vein starts a fresh assessment, due immediately like crops.
rows.anchor: فقال مالك وأصحابه: لا شيء فيما يخرج من المعادن من ذهب أو فضة

rows.speaker: سحنون
rows.claim: Sahnun says a person's separate mines are not combined; each mine is assessed only when it independently reaches 200 dirhams or twenty dinars.
rows.anchor: قال سحنون في رجل له معادن: إنه لا يضم ما في واحد منها إلى غيرها

rows.speaker: محمد بن مسلمة
rows.claim: Ibn Maslama says separate mines are combined and assessed together, like crops.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن مسلمة: يضم بعضها إلى بعض ويزكى الجميع كالزرع

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and his companions treat minerals like rikaz: after a fifth, gold or silver is zakatable at the threshold after a year, combining with existing holdings; al-Thawri agrees.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة وأصحابه: المعدن كالركاز

rows.speaker: المزني
rows.claim: Al-Muzani says al-Shafi'i hesitated over minerals but that his principles suggest treating extraction as a windfall, taxed after a year; al-Layth, al-Shafi'i as transmitted by al-Muzani, Dawud, and his followers hold this view.
rows.anchor: وذكر المزني عن الشافعي قال: وأما الذي أنا واقف فيه فما يخرج من المعادن

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The jurists cite the hadith that newly acquired property owes no zakat until a year passes; al-Tirmidhi and al-Daraqutni transmit it.
rows.anchor: لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i cites a report from Abu Sa'id that the Prophet gave a small gold nugget in its soil to people whose hearts were to be reconciled, sent by Ali from Yemen; he takes this as evidence that mines follow zakat rules.
rows.anchor: واحتجوا أيضا بما رواه عبد الرحمن بن أنعم عن أبي سعيد الخدري: أن النبي

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik cites a report that the Prophet granted Bilal ibn al-Harith the Qabaliyya mines, from which only zakat is still taken; its Rabi'a chain is disconnected and not acceptable to hadith specialists, though it is used as Medinese practice.
rows.anchor: وحجة مالك حديث عن ربيعة بن أبي عبد الرحمن أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أقطع بلال ابن الحارث المعادن القبلية

rows.speaker: البزار
rows.claim: Al-Bazzar records a second grant version through al-Darawardi and another through Kathir ibn Abdullah describing the mines and cultivable land; the latter transmitter is widely judged weak.
rows.anchor: ورواه الدراوردي عن ربيعة عن الحارث بن بلال المزني عن أبيه. ذكره البزار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of earth extraction is complete here; the sea's produce is treated in al-Nahl, and the animal-injury hadith is revisited in al-Anbiya.
rows.anchor: هذا حكم ما أخرجته الأرض، وسيأتي في سورة «النحل» حكم ما أخرجه البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tayammum means to intend or aim; poetic evidence is deferred to al-Nisa, and the verse shows that earnings can be good or bad.
rows.anchor: تيمموا معناه تقصدوا، وستأتي الشواهد من أشعار العرب

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة بن سهل
rows.claim: Abu Umama ibn Sahl identifies the forbidden inferior dates as jaʿrūr and a variety called lawn ḥabīq; the Prophet prohibited taking them as zakat.
rows.anchor: وروى النسائي عن أبى أمامة ابن سهل بن حنيف

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: In a report from Abu Umama's father, someone brought an inferior bunch of dates for charity; the Prophet asked who brought it, and the verse was revealed. The Prophet then barred jaʿrūr and ḥabīq dates from zakat.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri identifies the two forbidden types as varieties of dates from Medina; al-Tirmidhi transmits the al-Bara report and authenticates it.
rows.anchor: قال الزهري: لونين من تمر المدينة وأخرجه الترمذي من حديث البراء وصححه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and al-Nahhas report Ibn Masud's reading 'wa-la taʾammamū'; the author treats it as a dialectal variant.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري والنحاس أن في قراءة عبد الله «ولا تأمموا»

rows.speaker: مسلم بن جندب
rows.claim: Muslim ibn Jundub reads the verb with a ḍamma on tāʾ and kasra on mīm; Ibn Kathir doubles tāʾ, and other authorities report further hamza and gemination variants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مسلم بن جندب «ولا تيمموا» بضم التاء وكسر الميم

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani reports one parsing that ends the sentence at 'the bad'; 'from it you spend' then describes the inferior item and rebukes people for accepting it only by overlooking its defects.
rows.anchor: قال الجرجاني في كتاب «نظم القرآن»: قال فريق من الناس:

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: A second parsing keeps the sentence connected through 'from it'; the pronoun returns to earnings, and 'you spend' can be a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: فالضمير في «منه» عائد على «ماكسبتم»

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara, Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak say people would accept inferior goods in settling debts only by compromising their rights, so they should not offer God what they dislike for themselves.
rows.anchor: قال معناه البراء بن عازب وابن عابس والضحاك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says people would buy the inferior item in the market only at a discount; Ali reportedly gives a similar explanation. Ibn Atiyya says these readings fit obligatory zakat.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: معنى الآية: ولستم بآخذيه

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi argues that if the verse concerned obligatory zakat, inferior property could never be accepted even by compromise; only voluntary charity could be accepted without overlooking defects.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: لو كانت في الفرض لما قال

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara also says a recipient would accept such a poor gift only out of embarrassment; Ibn Atiyya takes this as fitting voluntary charity. Ibn Zayd reads it as tolerating the reprehensibility of unlawful property.
rows.anchor: وقال البراء بن عازب أيضا معناه: «ولستم بآخذيه»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fragmentary verse says some people accept humiliation by overlooking a defect, supporting the lexical sense of lenience.
rows.anchor: أناس يرضون بالإغماض وقد يحتمل أن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed derivation of 'overlook' is closing one's eyes to something unpleasant, like the cited poet who says he shuts his eyes to troubling matters without being blind.
rows.anchor: وقد يحتمل أن يكون منتزعا إما من تغميض العين لأن الذي يريد الصبر على مكروه يغمض عينيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed derivation connects aghmada with going to an obscure place, as in expressions for traveling to Oman, Iraq, Najd, or Tihama; the phrase then implies interpretive effort to accept the item.
rows.anchor: وإما من قول العرب: أغمض الرجل إذا أتى غامضا من الأمر

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri has a light reading with fatḥa on tāʾ and kasra on mīm, and another doubled reading; the first suggests negotiating the price down and the second accepting at a discount, according to al-Nahhas and Abu Amr al-Dani.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري بفتح التاء وكسر الميم مخففا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada is reported to read the verb with ḍamma on tāʾ, still ghayn, and light mīm, meaning that a discount is made for you; Ibn Jinni explains the form as finding oneself to have overlooked the matter.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة أيضا «تغمضوا» بضم التاء وسكون الغين وفتح الميم مخففا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the mainstream reading can mean either to excuse a defect, close the eye to it, or accept an obscure interpretation, whether the property is unlawful or an unwanted gift or debt payment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقراءة الجمهور تخرج على التجاوز وعلى تغميض العين

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi says the reading means closing the eyes of one's insight to accepting the inferior item.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: ومن قرأ «تغمضوا» فالمعنى تغمضون أعين بصائركم

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines ghamḍ as leniency in buying or selling; 'make an allowance for me' asks the seller to lower the price because of poor quality.
rows.anchor: قال الجوهري: وغمضت عن فلان إذا تساهلت عليه في بيع أو شراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle an is accusative here, with an implied meaning 'except by doing so.'
rows.anchor: «أن» في موضع نصب، والتقدير إلا بأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is free of need for donations; whoever seeks reward should give something valuable, since the benefit is for the donor, and God is praised in every state.
rows.anchor: على صفة الغنى، أي لا حاجة به إلى صدقاتكم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God did not command charity out of need; He informed people that He is praiseworthy for all His blessings.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج في قوله «واعلموا أن الله غني حميد»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's promise means frightening people with poverty so they will not spend; the verse follows the charity teaching because Satan discourages spending for God and urges sins, including spending on sins.
rows.anchor: معناه يخوفكم «الفقر» أي بالفقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that Satan urges people not to give, leading them to disobedience and severed kinship.
rows.anchor: أي بأن لا تتصدقوا فتعصوا وتتقاطعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word faqr is also read with a ḍamma on the first letter, like the dialectal variants for weakness.
rows.anchor: وقرىء «الفقر» بضم الفاء وهي لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary Arabic, an unqualified promise concerns good; when the promised content is specified, it can refer to good or evil, and this verse uses promise in both senses.
rows.anchor: الوعد في كلام العرب إذا أطلق فهو في الخير، وإذا قيد بالموعود

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse contains two promises from God and two from Satan.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: في هذه الآية اثنتان من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports the Prophet's distinction between Satan's prompt, which threatens evil and denies truth, and the angel's prompt, which promises good and affirms truth; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Outside Qur'anic recitation, one can say 'command you evil' without the preposition bā; Sibawayh cites a poem with the same construction.
rows.anchor: بحذف الباء وأنشد سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maghfira is God's covering of people in this world and the next; faḍl is provision and expansion in this world and bliss in the next.
rows.anchor: والمغفرة هي الستر على عباده في الدنيا والآخرة.

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash notes that some infer poverty is better than wealth because Satan's fear of poverty turns people away from good; Ibn Atiyya says this is not decisive and has a strong counterargument.
rows.anchor: ذكر النقاش أن بعض الناس تأنس بهذه الآية في أن الفقر أفضل من الغنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Torah saying promises expanded favor to the servant who spends from God's provision, and Ibn Abbas cites 34:39 as its Qur'anic confirmation: God replaces what is spent and is the best provider.
rows.anchor: في التوراة «عبدي أنفق من رزقي أبسط عليك فضلي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas cites the promise that whatever people spend God replaces, and that He is the best provider; the author adds that 'vast, knowing' describes generous giving and knowledge of its proper recipients and all things.
rows.anchor: ذكره ابن عباس. { والله واسع عليم } تقدم معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's being vast and knowing means He gives from abundance, knows where to place His gift, and knows both the unseen and seen.
rows.anchor: { والله واسع عليم } تقدم معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word mā can be a verbal noun or a relative pronoun with an omitted object pronoun; 'like a wind' means like a gust of wind.
rows.anchor: «ما» تصلح أن تكون مصدرية، وتصلح أن تكون بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says ṣirr is severe cold; one etymology connects it to the sound of a harsh wind.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: والصر البرد الشديد. قيل: أصله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ṣirr is the sound of flames in the wind.
rows.anchor: الزجاج: هو صوت لهب النار التي كانت في تلك الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse compares disbelievers' spending, which is void and useless, to a crop destroyed by cold wind or fire after its owners expected a harvest; the meaning was also treated in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الآية: مثل نفقة الكافرين في بطلانها وذهابها

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says he forbade eating locusts killed by ṣirr; the commentary does not give a grading here.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: إنه نهى عن الجراد الذي قتله الصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God did not wrong the disbelievers; they wronged themselves through disbelief, disobedience, and withholding God's due. Another explanation says they sowed in the wrong season or place and were disciplined for misplacing things.
rows.anchor: بالكفر والمعصية ومنع حق الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra supply an omitted object: people should not suppose stinginess is good for them; the omission is signaled by the verb 'are stingy.'
rows.anchor: قال الخليل وسيبويه والفراء: المعنى البخل خيرا لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted noun is illustrated by 'whoever is truthful, it is better for him,' where 'truth' is understood from 'truthful'; a poem similarly uses 'fool' to imply folly.
rows.anchor: لدلالة يبخلون على البخل وهو كقوله

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas calls Hamza's second-person reading very remote; it can be parsed as forbidding one to consider the stinginess of the stingy good, like 'ask the village.'
rows.anchor: وأما قراءة حمزة بالتاء فبعيدة جدا قاله النحاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun huwa is an emphatic separator for Basran grammarians and a supporting particle for Kufans; it can also be the subject of a nominal sentence meaning 'it is better for them.'
rows.anchor: فاصلة عند البصريين، وهي العماد عند الكوفيين

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says the sīn in 'they will be collared' signals a threat: they will be made to wear it later.
rows.anchor: سين الوعيد، أي سوف يطوقون قاله المبرد

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Wa'il, Abu Malik, al-Suddi, al-Sha'bi, and others say the verse concerns withholding wealth, spending in God's path, and obligatory zakat; Abu Hurayra reports the zakat-evader transformed into a bald serpent that collars him and says, 'I am your wealth, your treasure.'
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية نزلت في البخل بالمال والإنفاق في سبيل الله، وأداء الزكاة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masud says anyone who withholds zakat will be made into a bald snake that collars him; the Prophet recites this verse as proof. Ibn Majah transmits it.
rows.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet says a miser who refuses a relative's request for surplus wealth will be brought on Judgment Day as a panting fire-serpent that collars him; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وجاء عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and other scholars say the verse instead concerns the People of the Book concealing what they knew about Muhammad; on this reading, 'will be collared' means they will bear punishment, from the sense of capacity in 2:184.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: إنما نزلت في أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i says they will be given a fiery collar on Judgment Day, an interpretation that fits the financial reading.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم النخعي: معنى { سيطوقون } سيجعل لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that people will be bound to their deeds as a neck is bound by a collar, paralleling 17:13; a poem by Abdullah ibn Jahsh to Abu Sufyan uses the image of burdening someone like a dove's collar.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يلزمون أعمالهم كما يلزم الطوق العنق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bukh is withholding a right that is due; refusing something not owed is not blameworthy. Hijaz and other Arabs differ in the verb's morphology.
rows.anchor: والبخل والبخل في اللغة أن يمنع الإنسان الحق الواجب عليه

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas notes that Hijaz speakers say yabkhalūna/bakhilū, while other Arabs use the other conjugation; Ibn Faris gives additional noun and verb forms.
rows.anchor: وأهل الحجاز يقولون: يبخلون وقد بخلوا. وسائر العرب يقولون:

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: In a report cited by al-Mawardi, the Prophet asks the Ansar to name their leader; when they name the stingy Jad ibn Qays, he says no disease is worse than miserliness and tells a story of hosts avoiding guests until men and women become sexually occupied with their own sex.
rows.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال للأنصار: «من سيدكم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Views differ on whether bukh and shuḥḥ are synonymous: bukh is withholding what one has, while shuḥḥ is eagerness to acquire what one lacks; another says shuḥḥ is greed, which the author prefers.
rows.anchor: واختلف في البخل والشح هل هما بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Jabir reports the Prophet warning against injustice and greed, which destroyed earlier peoples, led them to bloodshed, and made them violate sacred things; Muslim transmits it.
rows.anchor: لما رواه مسلم عن جابر بن عبد الله أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This report refutes the claim that shuḥḥ is only refusal of recommended charity: that would not merit such severe warnings and ruin in both worlds.
rows.anchor: إن البخل منع الواجب، والشح منع المستحب

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports a Prophetic statement that fighting dust and Hell's smoke never meet in a Muslim's nostrils, nor do faith and greed coexist; al-Nasa'i transmits it.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning shows shuḥḥ is more blameworthy than bukh, although a report that a believer cannot be miserly suggests a degree of equivalence.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن الشح أشد في الذم من البخل إلا أنه قد جاء ما يدل على مساواتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God says He will inherit the heavens and earth: after creation and ownership disappear, He remains; human inheritance is only an analogy, since God already owned everything and human wealth was a loan returned to its owner.
rows.anchor: أخبر تعالى ببقائه ودوام ملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel in 19:40 teaches people to spend before death rather than leave their wealth as God's inheritance; only what they spent benefits them.
rows.anchor: والمعنى في الآيتين أن الله تعالى أمر عباده بأن ينفقوا ولا يبخلوا قبل أن يموتوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah closes by commanding reflection on God's signs in creation; this makes faith rest on certainty and evidence rather than imitation, since the signs proceed from the living, sustaining, powerful, holy, self-sufficient God.
rows.anchor: فختم تعالى هذه السورة بالأمر بالنظر والاستدلال في آياته إذ لا تصدر إلا عن حي قيوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People of understanding are those who use their minds to contemplate proofs.
rows.anchor: الذين يستعملون عقولهم في تأمل الدلائل

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Aisha reports that after this verse was revealed, the Prophet prayed and wept; when Bilal asked why, he said he should be a grateful servant and warned that woe awaits one who recites without reflecting. No grading is stated here.
rows.anchor: على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قام يصلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars recommend wiping the face on waking and beginning night prayer by reciting these ten verses, following the Prophet, then praying what one can; reflection joined to action is the best work discussed here.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء: يستحب لمن انتبه من نومه أن يمسح على وجهه

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet read ten verses from the end of Al-Imran each night; al-Wa'ili transmits it through Sulayman ibn Musa, Muzahir ibn Aslam, and al-Maqburi, with no grading stated.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي هريرة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقرأ عشر آيات

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: A report from Uthman says whoever recites the end of Al-Imran at night is credited with spending the whole night in prayer.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم أول السورة عن عثمان قال: من قرأ آخر آل عمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Standing, sitting, and lying on one's side represent the three states that occupy nearly all human time; Aisha says the Prophet remembered God at all times, including in the toilet, according to the author’s application.
rows.anchor: ذكر تعالى ثلاث هيئات لا يخلوا ابن آدم منها في غالب أمره

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet remembered God in every circumstance; Muslim transmits the report.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا المعنى قول عائشة رضي الله عنها:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: Scholars differ on remembering God in the toilet: Abdullah ibn Amr, Ibn Sirin, and al-Nakha'i permit it; Ibn Abbas, Ata, and al-Sha'bi dislike it. The author prefers permission based on the verse and hadith's general wording.
rows.anchor: وقد اختلف العلماء في هذا فأجاز ذلك عبد الله بن عمرو وابن سيرين والنخعي

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakha'i says there is no harm in remembering God in the toilet because the remembrance rises, meaning angels carry it written in their records; 50:18 supports the scribes' recording.
rows.anchor: قال النخعي: لا بأس بذكر الله في الخلاء فإنه يصعد.
